steps.title: Top of the South Island
steps.body: Marlborough lies at the north-east tip of New Zealand's South Island, around the town of Blenheim. It's New Zealand's largest wine region by far, with about 30,000 hectares, around two-thirds of the country's vineyards. Its main valleys are the broad Wairau Valley and the smaller, higher Awatere Valley, separated by hills.
steps.highlight: About two-thirds of New Zealand's vines

steps.title: Bright and cool
steps.body: Marlborough is one of New Zealand's sunniest places, with long days and strong ultraviolet light, sheltered from westerly rain by mountains. Nights are cold, so the day and night range is wide. Grapes ripen slowly over a long season, keeping high acidity and intense aromas. Stony, free-draining alluvial soils from old riverbeds limit vigour. Spring frost is a risk.

steps.prompt: What gives Marlborough wines both ripeness and high acidity?
steps.explanation: A wide day and night range keeps acidity while sun ripens the fruit.

steps.title: Fast growth
steps.body: Commercial vines were first planted in Marlborough in 1973, by Montana, now Brancott Estate. In 1985, Cloudy Bay's first Sauvignon Blanc drew worldwide attention. From a few hundred hectares, the region grew to the largest in the country within 40 years, driven by export demand.

steps.prompt: Marlborough is New Zealand's largest wine region.
steps.explanation: Yes, with around two-thirds of the country's vineyards.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Marlborough sits at the top of the South Island, around Blenheim
Sunny days and cold nights give ripe fruit and high acidity
Planted from 1973, it grew fast after Cloudy Bay's 1985 success
